passages.title: From Adam to Israel and Edom
passages.summary: The book opens with a list of names and no story. It runs from Adam through Noah to Noah’s three sons. It names the peoples that came from Japheth, Ham, and Shem. Shem’s line leads to Abraham. Abraham’s sons are Isaac and Ishmael, with more sons by Keturah. Isaac’s sons are Esau and Israel. The rest of the chapter lists Esau’s family and the kings and chiefs of Edom.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and wide regions. The family lists do not describe journeys between them.

lds.text: Why might the book begin with Adam instead of David?

contextNote.title: Names place a small community in a larger past
contextNote.text: Verse 1 is three names with no verb. The list assumes readers know the stories from Genesis. It starts with all humanity before it narrows. Verses 5–23 name many nations, and only then comes Abraham (verse 27). Verse 34 uses the name Israel, not Jacob. Edom, Israel’s neighbor and rival, receives twenty verses (verses 35–54). The book sets one people’s history inside the history of everyone.

passages.title: Judah’s families and David’s ancestors
passages.summary: The chapter lists the twelve sons of Israel and then follows Judah. Judah’s first sons were born to a Canaanite woman. Tamar, his daughter-in-law, bore him Perez and Zerah. The line of Perez runs through Boaz and Jesse to David, the seventh son. David’s sisters and their warrior sons are named. Long lists follow for Caleb’s and Jerahmeel’s families. One man with no sons gives his daughter to his Egyptian servant. The chapter ends with families of scribes who were Kenites.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and wide regions. The family lists do not describe journeys between them.

lds.text: Which women and people from other lands appear in Judah’s family?

contextNote.title: The family record includes work as well as descent
contextNote.text: Verse 55 ends Judah’s record with a trade and a foreign origin. These families were scribes, and they were Kenites. Judges 1:16 says the Kenites came from Moses’s in-laws. The chapter has already named a Canaanite mother (verse 3). It names Tamar (verse 4) and an Ishmaelite father (verse 17). It records an Egyptian servant who married into the line (verses 34–35). The list of David’s own tribe makes no effort to hide outsiders.

passages.title: David’s children and the royal line after exile
passages.summary: The chapter lists David’s sons born in Hebron and in Jerusalem. It names his daughter Tamar. Then it lists the kings of Judah from Solomon to Josiah’s sons. Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin, is named “the captive.” His sons include Shealtiel and Pedaiah. Zerubbabel appears in the next generation. The list continues for several generations after the exile.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and wide regions. The family lists do not describe journeys between them.

lds.text: What hope might a surviving royal family give people after exile?

contextNote.title: The royal family line continues after royal defeat
contextNote.text: Verse 17 gives a king a new title: “the captive.” The list does not stop with him. Verses 17–24 carry David’s family on for generations with no throne. Zerubbabel in verse 19 later leads the return (Ezra 3:2). None of these men is called king. Yet each name is kept in order. Second Samuel 7:16 promised David a lasting house, and the list shows it surviving.

passages.title: Judah, Jabez, craftspeople, and Simeon’s settlements
passages.summary: The chapter adds more clans of Judah. A man named Jabez prays for blessing, more land, and protection from harm. God grants his request. The list names a valley of craftsmen, a guild of linen workers, and royal potters. Then it turns to Simeon’s towns in the south. Some Simeonites move to find pasture for their flocks. In Hezekiah’s time they take land at Gedor. Others defeat a remnant of Amalek at Mount Seir.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and wide regions. The family lists do not describe journeys between them.

lds.text: What does Jabez ask God to protect him from?

contextNote.title: Named occupations connect ancestry with ordinary provision
contextNote.text: This family list keeps a record of trades. Verse 14 names a valley of craftsmen. Verse 21 names families that worked fine linen. Verse 23 names potters who lived “with the king for his work.” So some families served in royal workshops. The list treats that work as worth remembering beside warriors and chiefs. A reader after the exile could trace a craft as well as a bloodline.

passages.title: Eastern tribes, prayer, and captivity
passages.summary: Reuben was Israel’s firstborn, but he lost the birthright by wronging his father. It passed to Joseph’s sons, while Judah produced the ruler. The chapter lists Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan. In a war with the Hagrites they cry to God, and he helps them. They take many animals and captives. Later these tribes are unfaithful and follow the gods of the land. God stirs up the king of Assyria, who carries them away.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and wide regions. The family lists do not describe journeys between them.

lds.text: The Seminary manual connects these passages with trust and repentance. Why did Reuben lose the birthright (verse 1)?

contextNote.title: Birth order does not explain every inherited role
contextNote.text: Verse 1 pauses the list to explain an oddity. Reuben was born first, yet he is not listed first. Genesis 35:22 and 49:3–4 record his offense. Verses 1–2 then divide three kinds of first place. Reuben keeps the birth order, and Joseph gets the birthright. Judah gets the ruler. The verses show that standing in this family did not rest on birth alone.

passages.title: Levi’s families, singers, priests, and towns
passages.summary: This chapter lists the families of Levi. It traces the high priests from Aaron to the exile. It gives the families of Gershom, Kohath, and Merari. The prophet Samuel appears in the line of Kohath. David appointed Heman, Asaph, and Ethan to lead the singing. Other Levites did the remaining work of the tabernacle. Aaron’s sons alone served at the altars. The chapter ends with the towns given to the Levites in every tribe.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and wide regions. The family lists do not describe journeys between them.

lds.text: How do the singers’ duties differ from the priests’ duties?

contextNote.title: Shared ancestry contains different forms of sacred work
contextNote.text: All the people in this chapter descend from Levi. Their work is not the same. Verses 31–32 say David set the singers in place. Verse 48 gives other Levites the general service of the tent. Verse 49 keeps the altars and atonement for Aaron and his sons. It says this follows what Moses commanded. So the chapter names two sources for these roles: Moses and David.

passages.title: Northern families, grief, and Sheerah’s building
passages.summary: The chapter lists families of Issachar, Benjamin, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Asher. It counts their fighting men. In Ephraim’s family, men of Gath kill sons who came to take cattle. Ephraim mourns many days, and his brothers come to comfort him. He names his next son Beriah because of the trouble. His daughter Sheerah builds three towns. Joshua son of Nun comes from this line.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and wide regions. The family lists do not describe journeys between them.

lds.text: Which work by women does this family list remember?

contextNote.title: A woman's building work receives a place in family memory
contextNote.text: Verse 24 sits between a story of grief and Joshua’s ancestry. It says Sheerah built Lower and Upper Beth Horon. A third town, Uzzen Sheerah, carries her name. The Bible rarely credits a woman with building towns. The list gives no further detail about her. Verses 21–23 have just told of sons killed and a father’s mourning. The family record keeps the loss and the building side by side.

passages.title: Benjamin’s families and Saul’s descendants
passages.summary: The chapter gives a long list of Benjamin’s families. Some heads of families lived in Jerusalem. Others lived at Gibeon. The list reaches Ner, Kish, and Saul. Saul’s sons include Jonathan and Eshbaal. Jonathan’s line continues through Merib-baal and Micah for many generations. The last family named has sons who were skilled archers.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and wide regions. The family lists do not describe journeys between them.

lds.text: How does Saul’s family list prepare for the next part of the book?

contextNote.title: The later defeated king still belongs within the recorded family
contextNote.text: Verse 33 names Israel’s first king in a plain family line. Chapter 10 will tell of his death and judge him. Yet verses 34–40 follow Jonathan’s descendants for twelve more generations. The kingdom passed to David, and the family did not vanish. Samuel calls two of these men Ishbosheth and Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 2:8; 9:6). David’s kindness to Jonathan’s son is one reason the line survived. The list keeps a defeated house within Israel’s record.

passages.title: Jerusalem’s residents and sanctuary workers
passages.summary: All Israel was listed, and Judah was exiled for unfaithfulness. The chapter names the first people who lived again in Jerusalem. They come from Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh. Priests, Levites, and temple servants are counted. Gatekeepers guard the four sides of God’s house. Some Levites count the vessels, and others care for flour, wine, oil, and spices. One bakes the flat bread, and singers serve day and night. Saul’s family list is repeated at the end.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and wide regions. The family lists do not describe journeys between them.

lds.text: What daily tasks keep the temple’s worship working?

contextNote.title: Sanctuary access requires work that often remains unseen
contextNote.text: Verse 26 calls the gatekeepers’ work “an office of trust.” The verses around it say what that meant day by day. They slept near the house and opened it each morning (verse 27). They counted the vessels in and out (verse 28). Others looked after flour, oil, and spices (verses 29–30). One man had charge of the baked offerings (verse 31). Verse 3 notes that northern tribes also lived in the restored city.

passages.title: Saul dies at Gilboa
passages.summary: The Philistines defeat Israel on Mount Gilboa. Saul’s three sons are killed, and archers wound him. He falls on his own sword. The Philistines strip him and put his head in the temple of Dagon. Men of Jabesh Gilead take the bodies and bury them. The writer says Saul died for his unfaithfulness. He did not keep the LORD’s word, and he consulted a medium. So the LORD gave the kingdom to David.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 1 Chronicles names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The Seminary manual uses Saul’s final notice to discuss trust and obedience. What three failures do verses 13–14 name?

contextNote.title: The account explains defeat through Saul’s conduct
contextNote.text: Chronicles reduces Saul’s whole reign to the day of his death. Verses 13–14 then add a verdict not found in this form in Samuel. They name three failures. He broke the LORD’s word, asked a medium, and did not ask the LORD. First Samuel 28:6 says Saul asked and received no answer. The two books describe the same end in different words. Seeking the LORD becomes a test for every later king in this book.

passages.title: David becomes king and his warriors are remembered
passages.summary: All Israel comes to Hebron and anoints David king. He captures Jebus, which is Jerusalem. Joab goes up first and becomes commander. The chapter then lists David’s mighty men. One stood his ground in a barley field against the Philistines. Three broke through enemy lines to bring David water from Bethlehem. Abishai and Benaiah are praised for their deeds. A long list of warriors follows, and it includes Uriah the Hittite.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 1 Chronicles names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Why does David refuse water that his men risk their lives to bring?

contextNote.title: A warrior's gift exposes the cost of royal wishes
contextNote.text: David speaks a wish in verse 17, and three men act on it. In verse 19 he refuses to drink what they brought. He calls the water their blood, because they risked their lives. He pours it out to the LORD (verse 18). The king will not enjoy a comfort bought at that price. Chronicles places the warriors at the start of David’s reign. Verse 10 says they made him king together with all Israel.

passages.title: Supporters gather to David
passages.summary: Fighting men join David while he hides from Saul at Ziklag. Some are from Benjamin, Saul’s own tribe. Men of Gad cross the Jordan in flood to reach him. The Spirit moves Amasai to pledge loyalty and peace to David. More men desert to him from Manasseh. At Hebron every tribe sends armed men to make him king. They feast with David for three days. Neighbors from far in the north bring food on donkeys, camels, mules, and oxen.

lds.text: How do David’s supporters help beyond bringing weapons?

contextNote.title: A gathered army also needs gathered food
contextNote.text: Verses 23–37 count soldiers tribe by tribe. Verse 40 turns to those who fed them. Food comes from as far as Issachar, Zebulun, and Naphtali. The verse lists flour, fig cakes, raisins, wine, oil, cattle, and sheep. An army of that size cannot gather without such supply. The verse ends with the reason: “there was joy in Israel.” Even Saul’s own tribe is counted among the supporters (verses 2 and 29).

passages.title: The first ark journey ends in fear
passages.summary: David consults his commanders and the whole assembly about the ark. All agree to bring it from Kiriath Jearim. They carry it on a new cart with music and singing. At a threshing floor the oxen stumble. Uzza puts out his hand to steady the ark, and God strikes him dead. David is angry and then afraid. He leaves the ark at the house of Obed-Edom. The LORD blesses that household for three months.

lds.text: Why does David stop moving the ark? What changes when he tries again?

contextNote.title: A failed journey interrupts confidence in royal planning
contextNote.text: The plan began with wide agreement. Verse 4 says it seemed right to all the people. Agreement did not make the method right. The ark rode on a cart, but the law required Levite carriers (Numbers 4:15). After Uzza’s death David asks the question in verse 12. He does not yet answer it. His answer comes in 15:13, after three months of thought.

passages.title: David’s house and victories against the Philistines
passages.summary: King Hiram of Tyre sends cedar and builders for David’s house. David sees that the LORD has established him for Israel’s sake. He takes more wives and has more children in Jerusalem. The Philistines raid the Valley of Rephaim. David asks God, attacks, and wins. The Philistines raid the same valley again. David asks again and is told to circle behind them. He waits for the sound of marching in the trees and wins.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 1 Chronicles names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Why does David ask for guidance before each battle?

contextNote.title: A repeated threat receives a different instruction
contextNote.text: The second raid looks like the first: same enemy, same valley (verse 13). David could have repeated what worked. Verse 14 says he “inquired again.” The answer is different this time. He must not go straight up but come around behind. Chapter 10:14 said Saul did not ask the LORD. Chronicles sets David’s habit of asking against that failure.

passages.title: Levites carry the ark with music
passages.summary: David prepares a tent for the ark in Jerusalem. He says only Levites may carry it. He gathers the priests and Levites and tells them to make themselves holy. They carry the ark on poles on their shoulders, as Moses commanded. David appoints singers and players of cymbals, harps, and lyres. God helps the Levites, and they offer sacrifices. All Israel brings up the ark with shouting and trumpets. Michal sees David dancing and despises him.

lds.text: What changes when David tries again to move the ark?

contextNote.title: A failed procession changes the next one
contextNote.text: Verse 13 is David’s answer to the question he asked in 13:12. He says “we,” and so includes himself in the fault. The fault was not carrying the ark as the rule required. Verses 2 and 15 state the correction: Levites, poles, and shoulders. Exodus 25:14 and Numbers 4:15 gave those instructions. The joy of the first attempt remains in the second. Now it is ordered, with named singers and leaders (verses 16–22).

passages.title: Thanksgiving and two centers of worship
passages.summary: The ark is set in its tent, and David offers sacrifices. He gives every person bread, meat, and raisins. He appoints Levites to thank and praise the LORD before the ark. Asaph and his brothers sing a psalm of thanks. It calls the nations to praise and recalls the covenant with Abraham. The people answer, “Amen.” David leaves Asaph to serve before the ark every day. Zadok and the priests offer the daily sacrifices at the tabernacle in Gibeon.

lds.text: The Seminary manual connects this song with continuing gratitude and praise. What work does David assign after the celebration (verse 37)?

contextNote.title: A public celebration becomes continuing assigned work
contextNote.text: The festival lasts a day. Verse 37 describes what continues after it. Asaph and his brothers must serve before the ark “continually.” The phrase “every day’s work” makes praise a regular duty. Verses 39–40 show a second site at Gibeon. The altar and the daily sacrifices stay there with Zadok. Worship remains divided between song and sacrifice until the temple is built.

passages.title: Nathan announces a house for David
passages.summary: David tells Nathan that he lives in cedar while the ark sits in a tent. Nathan tells him to do what is in his heart. That night God gives Nathan a different message. David will not build the house. God took him from the sheep and will build him a house instead. A son will build the temple, and his throne will last forever. David sits before the LORD and asks who he is to receive this. He prays that God will do as he has said.

lds.text: How does God’s promise change David’s plan for a temple?

contextNote.title: The proposed gift changes direction
contextNote.text: Nathan’s first answer in verse 2 is corrected within hours. Verse 4 is a plain refusal: “You shall not build.” Verse 10 turns the offer around. The LORD will build a house, a line of kings, for David. Second Samuel 7:14 warns that a sinning heir will be punished. Chronicles leaves that sentence out of verse 13. Verse 14 calls the kingdom God’s own.

passages.title: Victories, tribute, dedicated treasure, and officials
passages.summary: David defeats the Philistines and takes Gath. He defeats Moab, and the Moabites bring tribute. He defeats Hadadezer of Zobah and the Syrians who come to help. He takes gold shields and a great amount of bronze. Solomon later uses that bronze for the temple. King Tou of Hamath sends gifts. David dedicates all the silver and gold to the LORD. Abishai defeats Edom, and the chapter lists David’s officers.

lds.text: Where does David place the treasure gained from war?

contextNote.title: Military gain is assigned a sacred destination
contextNote.text: Verse 11 gives the spoil of five nations a destination. David dedicates it to the LORD. Verse 8 already looks ahead to the bronze sea and pillars. Chronicles ties David’s wars to the future temple. The same wars have another effect. In 22:8 they are the reason David himself may not build. War supplies the metal and also bars the builder.

passages.title: Humiliated envoys and war with Ammon
passages.summary: The king of Ammon dies, and David sends men to comfort his son Hanun. Hanun’s princes say the men have come to spy. Hanun shaves them and cuts off their clothes at the hips. David tells the shamed men to wait at Jericho. Ammon hires chariots and horsemen from Syria for a thousand talents of silver. Joab and Abishai fight on two fronts and win. The Syrians bring more troops from beyond the River. David defeats them, and they make peace.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me specifically compares this story with 2 Samuel 10–12. What do Hanun’s princes claim in verse 3?

contextNote.title: Advisers turn sympathy into suspected surveillance
contextNote.text: David’s message is sympathy for a death (verse 2). The princes in verse 3 turn it into spying. They give no evidence, and Hanun asks for none. The insult to the envoys makes war certain. Ammon then spends a fortune on hired armies (verses 6–7). Joab’s words in verse 13 leave the outcome to the LORD. The chapter follows 2 Samuel 10 closely.

passages.title: Rabbah falls and Philistine warriors die
passages.summary: In spring Joab leads the army against Ammon and besieges Rabbah. David stays in Jerusalem. Joab takes the city. David takes the heavy gold crown of its king and much plunder. He puts the people to work with saws, picks, and axes. Later wars with the Philistines follow. David’s men kill three giants, one of them Goliath’s brother. One giant has six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me notes that Chronicles omits negative stories about David. Compare verse 1 with 2 Samuel 11:1. What story does Chronicles leave out?

contextNote.title: Selection changes what a familiar period emphasizes
contextNote.text: Verse 1 matches the opening of 2 Samuel 11. Both say that David stayed in Jerusalem. Samuel then tells of Bathsheba, Uriah, and Nathan. Chronicles goes straight to the fall of Rabbah. It also omits Amnon, Tamar, and Absalom’s revolt. The writer does not say why. His interest in these chapters is David’s part in preparing the temple.

passages.title: Census, plague, and Ornan’s threshing floor
passages.summary: Satan moves David to count Israel. Joab objects but obeys, and he leaves out Levi and Benjamin. God is displeased and strikes Israel. The prophet Gad offers David three punishments. David chooses to fall into the LORD’s hand. A plague kills seventy thousand. David sees the angel standing over Jerusalem with a drawn sword. He buys Ornan’s threshing floor, builds an altar, and fire from heaven answers him.

lds.text: David asks why the people must suffer. What does his response show about responsibility?

contextNote.title: The king names the difference between command and cost
contextNote.text: Joab warned in verse 3 that the count would bring guilt on Israel. The king’s word prevailed (verse 4). In verse 17 David separates the command from its cost. He gave the order, and the people paid for it. He calls them “these sheep,” the language of a shepherd. He asks that the hand fall on him and his family. Second Samuel 24:1 describes the cause of the census differently.

passages.title: David prepares for Solomon’s temple
passages.summary: David says the threshing floor is the place for God’s house. He gathers stonecutters and stores up iron, bronze, and cedar. Solomon is young, so David prepares in great quantity. He tells Solomon that he wanted to build the house himself. The LORD refused because David had shed much blood. A son named Solomon, a man of rest, would build it. David hands over gold, silver, and workers. He orders Israel’s leaders to help his son.

lds.text: How does David help a task that someone else will finish?

contextNote.title: The future builder inherits resources and a restriction
contextNote.text: Second Samuel 7 gives no reason why David may not build. Verse 8 gives one: he has shed much blood in great wars. Verse 9 contrasts him with a son who will be a man of rest. David accepts the limit. He then does everything short of building. He chooses the site, stores materials, and hires workers (verses 1–5, 14–16). His work is to make another person’s work possible.

passages.title: Levitical service is organized
passages.summary: David is old and makes Solomon king. He counts the Levites aged thirty and above. There are thirty-eight thousand. Most will oversee the work of the LORD’s house. Others will be officers, judges, gatekeepers, and musicians. The families of Gershon, Kohath, and Merari are listed. The Levites will no longer carry the tabernacle. They will help the priests with courts, rooms, bread, flour, measures, and daily praise.

lds.text: Which temple duties involve ordinary food, measures, and supplies?

contextNote.title: A settled sanctuary changes the form of service
contextNote.text: Numbers 4 gave the Levites the work of carrying the tabernacle. Verse 25 says the LORD has given his people rest in Jerusalem. Verse 26 draws the result: nothing needs to be carried now. The Levites receive new duties suited to a fixed house (verses 28–32). These include cleaning, baking, and checking weights and sizes. They also stand to thank and praise each morning and evening. Verse 14 notes that Moses’s own sons served as ordinary Levites.

passages.title: Priestly divisions are assigned by lot
passages.summary: David organizes the priests, the sons of Aaron. Eleazar’s family has sixteen heads, and Ithamar’s has eight. They are divided by lot, since both families have leaders. A Levite scribe records the result before the king and the priests. Twenty-four divisions are named in order. The eighth lot falls to Abijah. The remaining Levites also cast lots for their duties. The chief’s household and the youngest brother’s are treated alike.

lds.text: How does drawing lots share duties among priestly families?

contextNote.title: Assignment by lot crosses differences in household status
contextNote.text: The priests’ turns of service are fixed by lot. Verse 5 gives the reason: both branches had officers of rank. A lot keeps either side from favoring its own. Verse 6 says a scribe wrote the results down before witnesses. Verse 31 extends the method to the other Levites. A leading household gets no better place than a younger brother’s. Luke 1:5 later names a priest from the division of Abijah (verse 10).

passages.title: Musicians, prophecy, and shared assignments
passages.summary: David and his commanders set apart musicians for the temple. They come from the families of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun. They are to prophesy with lyres, harps, and cymbals. Heman has fourteen sons and three daughters. All serve under their fathers’ direction. There are two hundred eighty-eight trained singers. They cast lots for their duties. Twenty-four groups of twelve are listed in order.

lds.text: Why does the music list include both teachers and students?

contextNote.title: Skill and learning belong within the same service system
contextNote.text: Verses 1–3 call the musicians’ work prophesying. The text treats temple song as speech from God as well as to him. Verse 7 says all two hundred eighty-eight were trained and skilled. Verse 8 then describes how duties were given out. The lot fell on small and great alike. Teacher and student stood in the same draw. Training belongs to the service, and rank earns no advantage.

passages.title: Gatekeepers, stored gifts, and public duties
passages.summary: The chapter lists the gatekeepers by family. Obed-Edom has sixty-two able descendants, for God blessed him. One father makes a younger son chief. Lots decide which family guards each gate. Guards are posted daily on every side. Other Levites keep the treasuries and the dedicated gifts. These gifts include spoil given by Samuel, Saul, Abner, and Joab. Still others serve as officers and judges across Israel.

lds.text: What does faithful care of temple supplies require?

contextNote.title: Stored gifts require named responsibility
contextNote.text: Verse 20 puts a named man over the treasures. The verses after it name more keepers and their families (verses 21–26). A named duty means someone answers for what is stored. Verses 27–28 list where the dedicated things came from. Samuel, Saul, Abner, and Joab all gave spoil. These men were rivals in life, and their gifts are kept together. Verse 24 places a descendant of Moses over the treasuries.

passages.title: Army rotations and royal property
passages.summary: The chapter lists the army’s twelve divisions. Each has twenty-four thousand men and serves one month a year. A leader is named for each tribe. David did not count those under twenty, since God promised many descendants. Stewards manage the king’s storehouses, fields, vineyards, and olive trees. Others manage herds, camels, donkeys, and flocks. Two of these stewards are foreigners. The king’s counselors are named last.

lds.text: Which workers support the kingdom through farming and storage?

contextNote.title: Royal strength depends on organized turns of service
contextNote.text: Verse 1 describes service “month by month.” Each division serves one month and goes home for eleven. The burden is shared in turns across the year. Verses 25–31 list the men who managed crops, wine, oil, and animals. An Ishmaelite keeps the camels, and a Hagrite keeps the flocks (verses 30–31). The kingdom depends on storekeepers and herdsmen as well as soldiers. Verses 23–24 recall the census that brought wrath.

passages.title: David gives Solomon plans and a charge
passages.summary: David gathers Israel’s leaders in Jerusalem and stands to speak. He wanted to build a house for the ark. God refused him as a man of war and chose Solomon. David charges Solomon to know God and serve him with a whole heart. He gives him the plans for every room and court. He gives the weights of gold and silver for each lampstand, table, and bowl. He says all of it came in writing from the LORD’s hand. He tells Solomon to be strong and do the work.

lds.text: The Seminary manual emphasizes seeking God and courage in service. What does David tell Solomon to do in verse 20?

contextNote.title: Receiving plans still leaves the next ruler work to do
contextNote.text: Solomon receives complete plans in verses 11–19. Verse 20 shows that plans do not finish a building. He must still “be strong and courageous, and do it.” Moses spoke nearly the same words to Joshua (Deuteronomy 31:7–8). The promise in the verse has a term: until the work is finished. Verse 9 states the condition that covers his whole life. Seeking God brings finding him, and leaving him brings rejection.

passages.title: Gifts, prayer, a new king, and David's death
passages.summary: David tells the assembly what he has given for the temple from his own treasure. The leaders give gold, silver, bronze, iron, and precious stones. The people rejoice because the gifts are given freely. David blesses the LORD before them all. He says everything in heaven and earth belongs to God. He asks God to keep the people’s hearts loyal and to help Solomon. Solomon is made king, and Zadok priest. David dies at a good old age, full of days, riches, and honor.

lds.text: The Seminary manual studies named records and revelation beyond the Bible. What do these records tell readers about David’s rule?

contextNote.title: Royal giving rests on a prior gift
contextNote.text: Verses 2–8 list gifts on a huge scale. In verse 14 David refuses to take credit for them. Everything comes from God, and the givers return what was his. Verse 15 calls Israel strangers and temporary residents, as their fathers were. The king says this while holding land, city, and throne. Verse 9 traces the people’s joy to giving willingly. Verse 17 says God tests the heart and is pleased with honesty.

events.title: From Adam to Israel and Edom
events.summary: The book opens with a list of names and no story. It runs from Adam through Noah to Noah’s three sons. It names the peoples that came from Japheth, Ham, and Shem. Shem’s line leads to Abraham. Abraham’s sons are Isaac and Ishmael, with more sons by Keturah. Isaac’s sons are Esau and Israel. The rest of the chapter lists Esau’s family and the kings and chiefs of Edom.
events.detail: Verse 1 is three names with no verb. The list assumes readers know the stories from Genesis. It starts with all humanity before it narrows. Verses 5–23 name many nations, and only then comes Abraham (verse 27). Verse 34 uses the name Israel, not Jacob. Edom, Israel’s neighbor and rival, receives twenty verses (verses 35–54). The book sets one people’s history inside the history of everyone.

events.title: Judah’s families and David’s ancestors
events.summary: The chapter lists the twelve sons of Israel and then follows Judah. Judah’s first sons were born to a Canaanite woman. Tamar, his daughter-in-law, bore him Perez and Zerah. The line of Perez runs through Boaz and Jesse to David, the seventh son. David’s sisters and their warrior sons are named. Long lists follow for Caleb’s and Jerahmeel’s families. One man with no sons gives his daughter to his Egyptian servant. The chapter ends with families of scribes who were Kenites.
events.detail: Verse 55 ends Judah’s record with a trade and a foreign origin. These families were scribes, and they were Kenites. Judges 1:16 says the Kenites came from Moses’s in-laws. The chapter has already named a Canaanite mother (verse 3). It names Tamar (verse 4) and an Ishmaelite father (verse 17). It records an Egyptian servant who married into the line (verses 34–35). The list of David’s own tribe makes no effort to hide outsiders.

events.title: David’s children and the royal line after exile
events.summary: The chapter lists David’s sons born in Hebron and in Jerusalem. It names his daughter Tamar. Then it lists the kings of Judah from Solomon to Josiah’s sons. Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin, is named “the captive.” His sons include Shealtiel and Pedaiah. Zerubbabel appears in the next generation. The list continues for several generations after the exile.
events.detail: Verse 17 gives a king a new title: “the captive.” The list does not stop with him. Verses 17–24 carry David’s family on for generations with no throne. Zerubbabel in verse 19 later leads the return (Ezra 3:2). None of these men is called king. Yet each name is kept in order. Second Samuel 7:16 promised David a lasting house, and the list shows it surviving.

events.title: Judah, Jabez, craftspeople, and Simeon’s settlements
events.summary: The chapter adds more clans of Judah. A man named Jabez prays for blessing, more land, and protection from harm. God grants his request. The list names a valley of craftsmen, a guild of linen workers, and royal potters. Then it turns to Simeon’s towns in the south. Some Simeonites move to find pasture for their flocks. In Hezekiah’s time they take land at Gedor. Others defeat a remnant of Amalek at Mount Seir.
events.detail: This family list keeps a record of trades. Verse 14 names a valley of craftsmen. Verse 21 names families that worked fine linen. Verse 23 names potters who lived “with the king for his work.” So some families served in royal workshops. The list treats that work as worth remembering beside warriors and chiefs. A reader after the exile could trace a craft as well as a bloodline.

events.title: Eastern tribes, prayer, and captivity
events.summary: Reuben was Israel’s firstborn, but he lost the birthright by wronging his father. It passed to Joseph’s sons, while Judah produced the ruler. The chapter lists Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan. In a war with the Hagrites they cry to God, and he helps them. They take many animals and captives. Later these tribes are unfaithful and follow the gods of the land. God stirs up the king of Assyria, who carries them away.

Verses 1–2 then divide three kinds of first place. Reuben keeps the birth order, and Joseph gets the birthright. Judah gets the ruler. The verses show that standing in this family did not rest on birth alone.

events.title: Levi’s families, singers, priests, and towns
events.summary: This chapter lists the families of Levi. It traces the high priests from Aaron to the exile. It gives the families of Gershom, Kohath, and Merari. The prophet Samuel appears in the line of Kohath. David appointed Heman, Asaph, and Ethan to lead the singing. Other Levites did the remaining work of the tabernacle. Aaron’s sons alone served at the altars. The chapter ends with the towns given to the Levites in every tribe.
events.detail: All the people in this chapter descend from Levi. Their work is not the same. Verses 31–32 say David set the singers in place. Verse 48 gives other Levites the general service of the tent. Verse 49 keeps the altars and atonement for Aaron and his sons. It says this follows what Moses commanded. So the chapter names two sources for these roles: Moses and David.

events.title: Northern families, grief, and Sheerah’s building
events.summary: The chapter lists families of Issachar, Benjamin, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Asher. It counts their fighting men. In Ephraim’s family, men of Gath kill sons who came to take cattle. Ephraim mourns many days, and his brothers come to comfort him. He names his next son Beriah because of the trouble. His daughter Sheerah builds three towns. Joshua son of Nun comes from this line.
events.detail: Verse 24 sits between a story of grief and Joshua’s ancestry. It says Sheerah built Lower and Upper Beth Horon. A third town, Uzzen Sheerah, carries her name. The Bible rarely credits a woman with building towns. The list gives no further detail about her. Verses 21–23 have just told of sons killed and a father’s mourning. The family record keeps the loss and the building side by side.

events.title: Benjamin’s families and Saul’s descendants
events.summary: The chapter gives a long list of Benjamin’s families. Some heads of families lived in Jerusalem. Others lived at Gibeon. The list reaches Ner, Kish, and Saul. Saul’s sons include Jonathan and Eshbaal. Jonathan’s line continues through Merib-baal and Micah for many generations. The last family named has sons who were skilled archers.
events.detail: Verse 33 names Israel’s first king in a plain family line. Chapter 10 will tell of his death and judge him. Yet verses 34–40 follow Jonathan’s descendants for twelve more generations. The kingdom passed to David, and the family did not vanish. Samuel calls two of these men Ishbosheth and Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 2:8; 9:6). David’s kindness to Jonathan’s son is one reason the line survived. The list keeps a defeated house within Israel’s record.

events.title: Jerusalem’s residents and sanctuary workers
events.summary: All Israel was listed, and Judah was exiled for unfaithfulness. The chapter names the first people who lived again in Jerusalem. They come from Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh. Priests, Levites, and temple servants are counted. Gatekeepers guard the four sides of God’s house. Some Levites count the vessels, and others care for flour, wine, oil, and spices. One bakes the flat bread, and singers serve day and night. Saul’s family list is repeated at the end.
events.detail: Verse 26 calls the gatekeepers’ work “an office of trust.” The verses around it say what that meant day by day. They slept near the house and opened it each morning (verse 27). They counted the vessels in and out (verse 28). Others looked after flour, oil, and spices (verses 29–30). One man had charge of the baked offerings (verse 31). Verse 3 notes that northern tribes also lived in the restored city.

events.title: Saul dies at Gilboa
events.summary: The Philistines defeat Israel on Mount Gilboa. Saul’s three sons are killed, and archers wound him. He falls on his own sword. The Philistines strip him and put his head in the temple of Dagon. Men of Jabesh Gilead take the bodies and bury them. The writer says Saul died for his unfaithfulness. He did not keep the LORD’s word, and he consulted a medium. So the LORD gave the kingdom to David.
events.detail: Chronicles reduces Saul’s whole reign to the day of his death. Verses 13–14 then add a verdict not found in this form in Samuel. They name three failures. He broke the LORD’s word, asked a medium, and did not ask the LORD. First Samuel 28:6 says Saul asked and received no answer. The two books describe the same end in different words. Seeking the LORD becomes a test for every later king in this book.

events.title: David becomes king and his warriors are remembered
events.summary: All Israel comes to Hebron and anoints David king. He captures Jebus, which is Jerusalem. Joab goes up first and becomes commander. The chapter then lists David’s mighty men. One stood his ground in a barley field against the Philistines. Three broke through enemy lines to bring David water from Bethlehem. Abishai and Benaiah are praised for their deeds. A long list of warriors follows, and it includes Uriah the Hittite.
events.detail: David speaks a wish in verse 17, and three men act on it. In verse 19 he refuses to drink what they brought. He calls the water their blood, because they risked their lives. He pours it out to the LORD (verse 18). The king will not enjoy a comfort bought at that price. Chronicles places the warriors at the start of David’s reign. Verse 10 says they made him king together with all Israel.

events.title: Supporters gather to David
events.summary: Fighting men join David while he hides from Saul at Ziklag. Some are from Benjamin, Saul’s own tribe. Men of Gad cross the Jordan in flood to reach him. The Spirit moves Amasai to pledge loyalty and peace to David. More men desert to him from Manasseh. At Hebron every tribe sends armed men to make him king. They feast with David for three days. Neighbors from far in the north bring food on donkeys, camels, mules, and oxen.
events.detail: Verses 23–37 count soldiers tribe by tribe. Verse 40 turns to those who fed them. Food comes from as far as Issachar, Zebulun, and Naphtali. The verse lists flour, fig cakes, raisins, wine, oil, cattle, and sheep. An army of that size cannot gather without such supply. The verse ends with the reason: “there was joy in Israel.” Even Saul’s own tribe is counted among the supporters (verses 2 and 29).

events.title: The first ark journey ends in fear
events.summary: David consults his commanders and the whole assembly about the ark. All agree to bring it from Kiriath Jearim. They carry it on a new cart with music and singing. At a threshing floor the oxen stumble. Uzza puts out his hand to steady the ark, and God strikes him dead. David is angry and then afraid. He leaves the ark at the house of Obed-Edom. The LORD blesses that household for three months.
events.detail: The plan began with wide agreement. Verse 4 says it seemed right to all the people. Agreement did not make the method right. The ark rode on a cart, but the law required Levite carriers (Numbers 4:15). After Uzza’s death David asks the question in verse 12. He does not yet answer it. His answer comes in 15:13, after three months of thought.

events.title: David’s house and victories against the Philistines
events.summary: King Hiram of Tyre sends cedar and builders for David’s house. David sees that the LORD has established him for Israel’s sake. He takes more wives and has more children in Jerusalem. The Philistines raid the Valley of Rephaim. David asks God, attacks, and wins. The Philistines raid the same valley again. David asks again and is told to circle behind them. He waits for the sound of marching in the trees and wins.
events.detail: The second raid looks like the first: same enemy, same valley (verse 13). David could have repeated what worked. Verse 14 says he “inquired again.” The answer is different this time. He must not go straight up but come around behind. Chapter 10:14 said Saul did not ask the LORD. Chronicles sets David’s habit of asking against that failure.

events.title: Levites carry the ark with music
events.summary: David prepares a tent for the ark in Jerusalem. He says only Levites may carry it. He gathers the priests and Levites and tells them to make themselves holy. They carry the ark on poles on their shoulders, as Moses commanded. David appoints singers and players of cymbals, harps, and lyres. God helps the Levites, and they offer sacrifices. All Israel brings up the ark with shouting and trumpets. Michal sees David dancing and despises him.
events.detail: Verse 13 is David’s answer to the question he asked in 13:12. He says “we,” and so includes himself in the fault. The fault was not carrying the ark as the rule required. Verses 2 and 15 state the correction: Levites, poles, and shoulders. Exodus 25:14 and Numbers 4:15 gave those instructions. The joy of the first attempt remains in the second. Now it is ordered, with named singers and leaders (verses 16–22).

events.title: Thanksgiving and two centers of worship
events.summary: The ark is set in its tent, and David offers sacrifices. He gives every person bread, meat, and raisins. He appoints Levites to thank and praise the LORD before the ark. Asaph and his brothers sing a psalm of thanks. It calls the nations to praise and recalls the covenant with Abraham. The people answer, “Amen.” David leaves Asaph to serve before the ark every day. Zadok and the priests offer the daily sacrifices at the tabernacle in Gibeon.
events.detail: The festival lasts a day. Verse 37 describes what continues after it. Asaph and his brothers must serve before the ark “continually.” The phrase “every day’s work” makes praise a regular duty. Verses 39–40 show a second site at Gibeon. The altar and the daily sacrifices stay there with Zadok. Worship remains divided between song and sacrifice until the temple is built.

events.title: Nathan announces a house for David
events.summary: David tells Nathan that he lives in cedar while the ark sits in a tent. Nathan tells him to do what is in his heart. That night God gives Nathan a different message. David will not build the house. God took him from the sheep and will build him a house instead. A son will build the temple, and his throne will last forever. David sits before the LORD and asks who he is to receive this. He prays that God will do as he has said.
events.detail: Nathan’s first answer in verse 2 is corrected within hours. Verse 4 is a plain refusal: “You shall not build.” Verse 10 turns the offer around. The LORD will build a house, a line of kings, for David. Second Samuel 7:14 warns that a sinning heir will be punished. Chronicles leaves that sentence out of verse 13. Verse 14 calls the kingdom God’s own.

events.title: Victories, tribute, dedicated treasure, and officials
events.summary: David defeats the Philistines and takes Gath. He defeats Moab, and the Moabites bring tribute. He defeats Hadadezer of Zobah and the Syrians who come to help. He takes gold shields and a great amount of bronze. Solomon later uses that bronze for the temple. King Tou of Hamath sends gifts. David dedicates all the silver and gold to the LORD. Abishai defeats Edom, and the chapter lists David’s officers.
events.detail: Verse 11 gives the spoil of five nations a destination. David dedicates it to the LORD. Verse 8 already looks ahead to the bronze sea and pillars. Chronicles ties David’s wars to the future temple. The same wars have another effect. In 22:8 they are the reason David himself may not build. War supplies the metal and also bars the builder.

events.title: Humiliated envoys and war with Ammon
events.summary: The king of Ammon dies, and David sends men to comfort his son Hanun. Hanun’s princes say the men have come to spy. Hanun shaves them and cuts off their clothes at the hips. David tells the shamed men to wait at Jericho. Ammon hires chariots and horsemen from Syria for a thousand talents of silver. Joab and Abishai fight on two fronts and win. The Syrians bring more troops from beyond the River. David defeats them, and they make peace.
events.detail: David’s message is sympathy for a death (verse 2). The princes in verse 3 turn it into spying. They give no evidence, and Hanun asks for none. The insult to the envoys makes war certain. Ammon then spends a fortune on hired armies (verses 6–7). Joab’s words in verse 13 leave the outcome to the LORD. The chapter follows 2 Samuel 10 closely.

He puts the people to work with saws, picks, and axes. Later wars with the Philistines follow. David’s men kill three giants, one of them Goliath’s brother. events.title: Census, plague, and Ornan’s threshing floor
events.summary: Satan moves David to count Israel. Joab objects but obeys, and he leaves out Levi and Benjamin. God is displeased and strikes Israel. The prophet Gad offers David three punishments. David chooses to fall into the LORD’s hand. A plague kills seventy thousand. David sees the angel standing over Jerusalem with a drawn sword. He buys Ornan’s threshing floor, builds an altar, and fire from heaven answers him.
events.detail: Joab warned in verse 3 that the count would bring guilt on Israel. The king’s word prevailed (verse 4). In verse 17 David separates the command from its cost. He gave the order, and the people paid for it. He calls them “these sheep,” the language of a shepherd. He asks that the hand fall on him and his family. Second Samuel 24:1 describes the cause of the census differently.

events.title: David prepares for Solomon’s temple
events.summary: David says the threshing floor is the place for God’s house. He gathers stonecutters and stores up iron, bronze, and cedar. Solomon is young, so David prepares in great quantity. He tells Solomon that he wanted to build the house himself. The LORD refused because David had shed much blood. A son named Solomon, a man of rest, would build it. David hands over gold, silver, and workers. He orders Israel’s leaders to help his son.
events.detail: Second Samuel 7 gives no reason why David may not build. Verse 8 gives one: he has shed much blood in great wars. Verse 9 contrasts him with a son who will be a man of rest. David accepts the limit. He then does everything short of building. He chooses the site, stores materials, and hires workers (verses 1–5, 14–16). His work is to make another person’s work possible.

events.title: Levitical service is organized
events.summary: David is old and makes Solomon king. He counts the Levites aged thirty and above. There are thirty-eight thousand. Most will oversee the work of the LORD’s house. Others will be officers, judges, gatekeepers, and musicians. The families of Gershon, Kohath, and Merari are listed. The Levites will no longer carry the tabernacle. They will help the priests with courts, rooms, bread, flour, measures, and daily praise.
events.detail: Numbers 4 gave the Levites the work of carrying the tabernacle. Verse 25 says the LORD has given his people rest in Jerusalem. Verse 26 draws the result: nothing needs to be carried now. The Levites receive new duties suited to a fixed house (verses 28–32). These include cleaning, baking, and checking weights and sizes. They also stand to thank and praise each morning and evening. Verse 14 notes that Moses’s own sons served as ordinary Levites.

events.title: Priestly divisions are assigned by lot
events.summary: David organizes the priests, the sons of Aaron. Eleazar’s family has sixteen heads, and Ithamar’s has eight. They are divided by lot, since both families have leaders. A Levite scribe records the result before the king and the priests. Twenty-four divisions are named in order. The eighth lot falls to Abijah. The remaining Levites also cast lots for their duties. The chief’s household and the youngest brother’s are treated alike.
events.detail: The priests’ turns of service are fixed by lot. Verse 5 gives the reason: both branches had officers of rank. A lot keeps either side from favoring its own. Verse 6 says a scribe wrote the results down before witnesses. Verse 31 extends the method to the other Levites. A leading household gets no better place than a younger brother’s. Luke 1:5 later names a priest from the division of Abijah (verse 10).

events.title: Musicians, prophecy, and shared assignments
events.summary: David and his commanders set apart musicians for the temple. They come from the families of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun. They are to prophesy with lyres, harps, and cymbals. Heman has fourteen sons and three daughters. All serve under their fathers’ direction. There are two hundred eighty-eight trained singers. They cast lots for their duties. Twenty-four groups of twelve are listed in order.

Verse 8 then describes how duties were given out. The lot fell on small and great alike. Teacher and student stood in the same draw. Training belongs to the service, and rank earns no advantage.

events.title: Gatekeepers, stored gifts, and public duties
events.summary: The chapter lists the gatekeepers by family. Obed-Edom has sixty-two able descendants, for God blessed him. One father makes a younger son chief. Lots decide which family guards each gate. Guards are posted daily on every side. Other Levites keep the treasuries and the dedicated gifts. events.detail: Verse 20 puts a named man over the treasures. The verses after it name more keepers and their families (verses 21–26). A named duty means someone answers for what is stored. Verses 27–28 list where the dedicated things came from. Samuel, Saul, Abner, and Joab all gave spoil. These men were rivals in life, and their gifts are kept together. events.title: Army rotations and royal property
events.summary: The chapter lists the army’s twelve divisions. Each has twenty-four thousand men and serves one month a year. A leader is named for each tribe. David did not count those under twenty, since God promised many descendants. Stewards manage the king’s storehouses, fields, vineyards, and olive trees. Others manage herds, camels, donkeys, and flocks. Two of these stewards are foreigners. The king’s counselors are named last.
events.detail: Verse 1 describes service “month by month.” Each division serves one month and goes home for eleven. The burden is shared in turns across the year. Verses 25–31 list the men who managed crops, wine, oil, and animals. An Ishmaelite keeps the camels, and a Hagrite keeps the flocks (verses 30–31). The kingdom depends on storekeepers and herdsmen as well as soldiers. Verses 23–24 recall the census that brought wrath.

events.title: David gives Solomon plans and a charge
events.summary: David gathers Israel’s leaders in Jerusalem and stands to speak. He wanted to build a house for the ark. God refused him as a man of war and chose Solomon. David charges Solomon to know God and serve him with a whole heart. He gives him the plans for every room and court. He gives the weights of gold and silver for each lampstand, table, and bowl. He says all of it came in writing from the LORD’s hand. He tells Solomon to be strong and do the work.
events.detail: Solomon receives complete plans in verses 11–19. Verse 20 shows that plans do not finish a building. He must still “be strong and courageous, and do it.” Moses spoke nearly the same words to Joshua (Deuteronomy 31:7–8). The promise in the verse has a term: until the work is finished. Verse 9 states the condition that covers his whole life. Seeking God brings finding him, and leaving him brings rejection.

events.title: Gifts, prayer, a new king, and David's death
events.summary: David tells the assembly what he has given for the temple from his own treasure. The leaders give gold, silver, bronze, iron, and precious stones. The people rejoice because the gifts are given freely. David blesses the LORD before them all. He says everything in heaven and earth belongs to God. He asks God to keep the people’s hearts loyal and to help Solomon. Solomon is made king, and Zadok priest. David dies at a good old age, full of days, riches, and honor.
events.detail: Verses 2–8 list gifts on a huge scale. In verse 14 David refuses to take credit for them. Everything comes from God, and the givers return what was his. Verse 15 calls Israel strangers and temporary residents, as their fathers were. The king says this while holding land, city, and throne. Verse 9 traces the people’s joy to giving willingly. Verse 17 says God tests the heart and is pleased with honesty.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Strong evidence supports this route. The line shows a general path. Its branches and exact roadbeds changed over time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The main connection is well supported. The line shows a broad route, not one fixed or fully built road.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The hill route is well supported. The exact track could divide or shift between nearby ridges and towns.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The valley route is well supported. The line combines several possible tracks. It does not mark specific river crossings.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional route is well supported. Local branches between valleys and fortified towns are simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass and connection are well supported. The line does not claim an exact roadbed at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Lachish–Jerusalem approaches
ancientRoads.summary: Routes through the Shephelah valleys connected Lachish with Jerusalem. They also joined nearby walled towns with the Judean hills.
ancientRoads.detail: Second Kings 18:17 sends an Assyrian army from Lachish up to Jerusalem. The text does not name the road. This line shows one common approach.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is probable. The exact track is unknown, so the line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection is well supported. The displayed bends are approximate and do not identify one preserved Iron Age roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: This broad route is well known. It was not one fully built road. Its path and local branches remain uncertain.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo route
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland route connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where many major routes met. They linked Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean. This line follows the broad route through the Orontes valley, not the desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is well supported. The evidence does not show one fixed Iron Age track. The line is dashed.

regions.name: Israel under David and Solomon · approximate
regions.summary: The Bible says Saul, David, and Solomon ruled all the tribes as one kingdom. Scholars disagree on how large it was.
regions.detail: David takes Jerusalem and makes it his capital (2 Samuel 5). Solomon builds the temple there, and the kingdom splits after his death.
regions.uncertainty: The shape covers the tribal lands from Dan to Beersheba. It leaves out lands that paid tribute.

regions.name: Philistine cities · approximate
regions.summary: Five Philistine cities held the southern coast: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, and Gath.
regions.detail: David defeats the Philistines after he becomes king (2 Samuel 5). Earlier he had lived among them at Gath and Ziklag.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Each city had its own ruler.

regions.name: Phoenician cities · approximate
regions.summary: Tyre, Sidon, and other coast cities each had their own king. They lived by ships and trade.
regions.detail: Hiram king of Tyre sends cedar and builders to David and Solomon. Solomon pays him in wheat and oil (1 Kings 5).
regions.uncertainty: The shape joins separate cities along one coast. They were never one kingdom.

regions.name: Aram of Damascus · approximate
regions.summary: Aram was a kingdom centered on Damascus. Assyria ended it in 732 BCE.
regions.detail: David defeats Aram of Damascus and puts garrisons there (2 Samuel 8:5–6). Rezon later rules Damascus against Solomon (1 Kings 11:23–25).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Aram and Israel traded control of Gilead and Bashan.

regions.name: Ammon · approximate
regions.summary: Ammon was a kingdom east of the Jordan. Its chief city was Rabbah, now Amman.
regions.detail: Ammon shames David’s messengers, and war follows (2 Samuel 10). Joab takes Rabbah in 2 Samuel 12.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the land around Rabbah.

regions.name: Moab · approximate
regions.summary: Moab was a kingdom on the high land east of the Dead Sea. Dibon was its capital.
regions.detail: David defeats Moab and makes it pay tribute (2 Samuel 8:2).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Numbers 21:26 says Moab once lost land north of the Arnon.

regions.name: Edom · approximate
regions.summary: Edom was a kingdom south of the Dead Sea. The Bible calls its people the children of Esau.
regions.detail: David puts garrisons in Edom (2 Samuel 8:14). Hadad of Edom later troubles Solomon (1 Kings 11).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Edom’s people later moved west into southern Judah.

regions.name: Egypt · approximate
regions.summary: Egypt’s kings ruled the Nile valley and delta.
regions.detail: Solomon marries Pharaoh’s daughter (1 Kings 3:1). Jeroboam flees to Shishak king of Egypt (1 Kings 11:40).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Egypt’s ruling families and power changed across these centuries.

guides.title: 1 Chronicles: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Names place a small community in a larger past
steps.text: Verse 1 is three names with no verb. The list assumes readers know the stories from Genesis. It starts with all humanity before it narrows. Verses 5–23 name many nations, and only then comes Abraham (verse 27). Verse 34 uses the name Israel, not Jacob. Edom, Israel’s neighbor and rival, receives twenty verses (verses 35–54). The book sets one people’s history inside the history of everyone.

steps.title: A failed procession changes the next one
steps.text: Verse 13 is David’s answer to the question he asked in 13:12. He says “we,” and so includes himself in the fault. The fault was not carrying the ark as the rule required. Verses 2 and 15 state the correction: Levites, poles, and shoulders. Exodus 25:14 and Numbers 4:15 gave those instructions. The joy of the first attempt remains in the second. Now it is ordered, with named singers and leaders (verses 16–22).

steps.title: Royal giving rests on a prior gift
steps.text: Verses 2–8 list gifts on a huge scale. In verse 14 David refuses to take credit for them. Everything comes from God, and the givers return what was his. Verse 15 calls Israel strangers and temporary residents, as their fathers were. The king says this while holding land, city, and throne. Verse 9 traces the people’s joy to giving willingly. Verse 17 says God tests the heart and is pleased with honesty.

chapterMaps.narrative: The book opens with a list of names and no story. It runs from Adam through Noah to Noah’s three sons. It names the peoples that came from Japheth, Ham, and Shem. Shem’s line leads to Abraham. Abraham’s sons are Isaac and Ishmael, with more sons by Keturah. Isaac’s sons are Esau and Israel. The rest of the chapter lists Esau’s family and the kings and chiefs of Edom.

chapterMaps.narrative: The chapter lists the twelve sons of Israel and then follows Judah. Judah’s first sons were born to a Canaanite woman. Tamar, his daughter-in-law, bore him Perez and Zerah. The line of Perez runs through Boaz and Jesse to David, the seventh son. David’s sisters and their warrior sons are named. Long lists follow for Caleb’s and Jerahmeel’s families. One man with no sons gives his daughter to his Egyptian servant. The chapter ends with families of scribes who were Kenites.

chapterMaps.narrative: The chapter lists David’s sons born in Hebron and in Jerusalem. It names his daughter Tamar. Then it lists the kings of Judah from Solomon to Josiah’s sons. Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin, is named “the captive.” His sons include Shealtiel and Pedaiah. Zerubbabel appears in the next generation. The list continues for several generations after the exile.

The list names a valley of craftsmen, a guild of linen workers, and royal potters. Then it turns to Simeon’s towns in the south. Some Simeonites move to find pasture for their flocks. In Hezekiah’s time they take land at Gedor. Others defeat a remnant of Amalek at Mount Seir.

chapterMaps.narrative: Reuben was Israel’s firstborn, but he lost the birthright by wronging his father. It passed to Joseph’s sons, while Judah produced the ruler. The chapter lists Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan. In a war with the Hagrites they cry to God, and he helps them. They take many animals and captives. Later these tribes are unfaithful and follow the gods of the land. God stirs up the king of Assyria, who carries them away.

The prophet Samuel appears in the line of Kohath. David appointed Heman, Asaph, and Ethan to lead the singing. Other Levites did the remaining work of the tabernacle. Aaron’s sons alone served at the altars. The chapter ends with the towns given to the Levites in every tribe.

In Ephraim’s family, men of Gath kill sons who came to take cattle. Ephraim mourns many days, and his brothers come to comfort him. He names his next son Beriah because of the trouble. His daughter Sheerah builds three towns. Joshua son of Nun comes from this line.

Saul’s sons include Jonathan and Eshbaal. Jonathan’s line continues through Merib-baal and Micah for many generations. The last family named has sons who were skilled archers.

They come from Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh. Priests, Levites, and temple servants are counted. Gatekeepers guard the four sides of God’s house. Some Levites count the vessels, and others care for flour, wine, oil, and spices. One bakes the flat bread, and singers serve day and night. Saul’s family list is repeated at the end.

chapterMaps.narrative: The Philistines defeat Israel on Mount Gilboa. Saul’s three sons are killed, and archers wound him. He falls on his own sword. The Philistines strip him and put his head in the temple of Dagon. Men of Jabesh Gilead take the bodies and bury them. The writer says Saul died for his unfaithfulness. He did not keep the LORD’s word, and he consulted a medium. So the LORD gave the kingdom to David.

One stood his ground in a barley field against the Philistines. Three broke through enemy lines to bring David water from Bethlehem. Abishai and Benaiah are praised for their deeds. A long list of warriors follows, and it includes Uriah the Hittite.

The Spirit moves Amasai to pledge loyalty and peace to David. More men desert to him from Manasseh. At Hebron every tribe sends armed men to make him king. They feast with David for three days. Neighbors from far in the north bring food on donkeys, camels, mules, and oxen.

At a threshing floor the oxen stumble. Uzza puts out his hand to steady the ark, and God strikes him dead. David is angry and then afraid. He leaves the ark at the house of Obed-Edom. The LORD blesses that household for three months.

He takes more wives and has more children in Jerusalem. The Philistines raid the Valley of Rephaim. David asks God, attacks, and wins. The Philistines raid the same valley again. David asks again and is told to circle behind them. He waits for the sound of marching in the trees and wins.

chapterMaps.narrative: David prepares a tent for the ark in Jerusalem. He says only Levites may carry it. He gathers the priests and Levites and tells them to make themselves holy. They carry the ark on poles on their shoulders, as Moses commanded. David appoints singers and players of cymbals, harps, and lyres. God helps the Levites, and they offer sacrifices. All Israel brings up the ark with shouting and trumpets. Michal sees David dancing and despises him.

Asaph and his brothers sing a psalm of thanks. It calls the nations to praise and recalls the covenant with Abraham. The people answer, “Amen.” David leaves Asaph to serve before the ark every day. Zadok and the priests offer the daily sacrifices at the tabernacle in Gibeon.

David will not build the house. God took him from the sheep and will build him a house instead. A son will build the temple, and his throne will last forever. David sits before the LORD and asks who he is to receive this. He prays that God will do as he has said.

He takes gold shields and a great amount of bronze. Solomon later uses that bronze for the temple. King Tou of Hamath sends gifts. David dedicates all the silver and gold to the LORD. Abishai defeats Edom, and the chapter lists David’s officers.

David tells the shamed men to wait at Jericho. Ammon hires chariots and horsemen from Syria for a thousand talents of silver. Joab and Abishai fight on two fronts and win. The Syrians bring more troops from beyond the River. David defeats them, and they make peace.

He puts the people to work with saws, picks, and axes. Later wars with the Philistines follow. David’s men kill three giants, one of them Goliath’s brother. One giant has six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot.

The prophet Gad offers David three punishments. David chooses to fall into the LORD’s hand. A plague kills seventy thousand. David sees the angel standing over Jerusalem with a drawn sword. He buys Ornan’s threshing floor, builds an altar, and fire from heaven answers him.

Solomon is young, so David prepares in great quantity. He tells Solomon that he wanted to build the house himself. The LORD refused because David had shed much blood. A son named Solomon, a man of rest, would build it. David hands over gold, silver, and workers. He orders Israel’s leaders to help his son.

The people rejoice because the gifts are given freely. David blesses the LORD before them all. He says everything in heaven and earth belongs to God. He asks God to keep the people’s hearts loyal and to help Solomon. Solomon is made king, and Zadok priest. David dies at a good old age, full of days, riches, and honor.
